definition: A model running in a loop with instructions and tools: at each step it either answers or asks to call a tool, your code runs the tool and returns the result, and the loop continues until the task is done. Its power and its risk both come from the tools - each call needs the user's authorisation, server-side validation and limits.
example: The shopping assistant looks up order 88213 with the shopper's token, sees it is delayed, and offers to start a return.

definition: The mechanism that lets a model use your code: each tool is described by a name, a description and a JSON schema, and the model returns a request to call one with specific arguments. The model never executes anything - your code decides whether to run the call, and must validate the arguments and authorise it like any API request.
example: The model returns getOrder with orderId 88213; the Shop API calls the orders tool with the shopper's token and returns the status.

definition: Microsoft Foundry's managed runtime for agents: it keeps conversation state, runs the tool loop, and offers built-in tools - file search, AI Search, code interpreter, web grounding, OpenAPI, Functions, Logic Apps and MCP - with identity, content safety and tracing. The runtime has no separate charge; you pay for tokens and tools.
example: The assistant agent lives in the assistant project, with three tools and its runs traced to Application Insights.

definition: An open standard for exposing tools and data to AI applications: an MCP server lists its tools with descriptions and schemas, and any MCP client - Foundry agents, GitHub Copilot, Copilot Studio - can discover and call them. Write a tool once and every agent can use it; Azure API Management can publish existing REST APIs as MCP servers with their policies intact.
example: The orders API is exposed as an MCP server through API Management, so the assistant and the service team's Copilot use the same, rate-limited tool.

definition: Microsoft's open-source SDK for building agents and multi-agent workflows in .NET and Python, succeeding Semantic Kernel and AutoGen. Use it, or a framework such as LangGraph, when you want the agent loop in your own code - custom state, several model providers, or orchestration patterns - rather than fully managed by Foundry Agent Service.
example: The returns team's internal tool runs a two-step Agent Framework workflow in its own API, calling a Foundry model.

definition: Splitting a task across several specialised agents coordinated in a pattern - sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat or a manager agent. Worth it when one agent's instructions and tools grow too large or parts need different permissions; otherwise it multiplies cost, latency and failure modes. Start with one agent.
example: A vendor's five-agent design is declined because one agent with three tools already passes the evaluation set.

definition: Designing an AI system so a person reviews or approves certain outputs or actions before they take effect - especially irreversible, costly or sensitive ones. The system prepares the action and pauses; the approval is logged. It is also how low-confidence extractions reach a reviewer.
example: The agent prepares refunds over £100 and posts them to the service team's Teams queue for approval.
